title: TB1-10045
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Turkey, claims refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

The specifics of the claim are set out in the narrative of the claimant's Personal Information Form2 (PIF); however the following is a summary. The claimant is a 22-year-old Kurdish (Kurmanji) young man who alleges a fear of persecution if returned to Turkey due to his political activities, his nationality and required military conscription.
I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity

The claimant's identity as a national of Turkey has been established by his testimony and by the personal identity documents filed, including a certified copy of his Turkish passport issued in XXXX 2010;3 his Turkish National Identity Card,4 a High School Student Identity Card5 and High School diploma.6 Credibility

When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are indeed true unless there is valid reason to doubt their veracity.7 The determination as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible is made on a balance of probabilities.8 The following aspects of the claimant's story did not establish credible evidence that, * He has the political profile he alleges; * He was detained by Turkish authorities in XXXX 2011 and/or sustained the mistreatment during this detention, or that; * Turkish authorities have any interest in him due to his political activities.

Rather, while I accept that the claimant may have participated in Newroz celebrations which may have resulted in his being detained by police while attending a Newroz celebration in XXXX 20069 and "at random" on XXXX XXXX, 200910 when police were attempting to disperse a protest in front of a court house, I have not been provided with credible or reliable evidence to establish that the claimant was even in Turkey in XXXX 2011. This consequently results in finding that the claimant has embellished the precipitating incident of XXXX XXXX, 201111 in efforts to bolster his claim for protection. Was the claimant in Turkey in XXXX 2011?

Having reviewed the evidence in its entirety, I find the claimant has not provided any credible evidence to support a finding that he was in Turkey as at the dates he has alleged, which is his responsibility to do. Newroz Celebration in XXXX 2011

The precipitating incident which the claimant has alleged was his reason for departing Turkey, as presented in his Personal Information Form and narrative is his having been arrested by police who attending a March 2011 Newroz celebration, attacking the crowd and arresting people at random. He states that he tried to run away but that he fell and twisted his foot and "that while he was on the ground that the police beat him with truncheons." The claimant's testimony indicated that he noticed the police arrive while he was dancing and described the police using tear gas, randomly catching people and beating whomever they caught. He indicated that he was rounded up with many other people and taken to a police station where he was put into a cell for two days, claiming that he was beaten and tortured until his father came to pick him up.

Having reviewed the evidence regarding this particular incident, I do not find that the claimant was individually targeted by the police for his perceived political opinion, or that he was tortured as he claims. Rather, the claimant's evidence is that he was dancing, enjoying the celebration when the police arrived. His evidence that police were arresting people at random clearly does not indicate that Turkish authorities had any personalized interest or were looking for him in particular. At minimum, I find that the claimant's oral testimony established that he was not "protesting" at the Newroz celebration as stated in information provided by him to immigration officials on XXXX XXXX, 2011.12 Notwithstanding, even if I were to accept that the claimant was in Turkey at that time and detained by police, which I do not, the claimant has not provided any corroborative evidence such as a police report or statement which he testified his father signed at his release to support this.

Further, given the torture the claimant alleges he sustained, he was asked if he sought medical attention for his injuries. He replied that, "his back was bad and his feet were swollen but he was afraid to go to the hospital and used traditional medicine instead." Consequently, whether the claimant was beaten and tortured has not been established by any independent corroborative evidence such as a medical report given he did not seek medical attention from a doctor nor did he attend a hospital because he was scared. Even if I were to accept that this incident and detention occurred, which I do not, I am unable to find credible that police would release the claimant after two days if they had any particular interest in him due to his political activities or more so due to any of his family members political activities or having been addressed by police as "traitors and separatists," as stated in his narrative.13 Indeed, counsel addressed the claimant's lack of evidence to support this incident.

Counsel asked the claimant the following: Q You testified that you have no proof of your detentions. Think again. Is there anything in personal documents to show you were detained? Not official documents but... A I have a letter from my brother in Canada. Q Why do you have no official document from the police? A The Turkish police don't' give you proof even when my father signed a paper. We were afraid to ask for it.

Notwithstanding counsel's subsequent questions and the claimant's responses that he had neither had any criminal charges laid against him nor was attended by a public prosecutor or taken to Court, this does not provide any corroborative evidence to support his allegation that he personally had been detained by police or indeed was in Turkey in XXXX 2011. The claimant, however, was able to provide corroborative evidence14 regarding the detention of person named 'XXXX XXXX,' which counsel indicates on the index page of the claimant's personal evidence II at item 515 is the claimant's brother XXXX XXXX. While I note that the claimant does have an older brother by this name as indicated in his PIF,16 the claimant had initially listed a different birth date than that as stated in the Court decision provided.

This decision from the State Security Court of XXXX, dated XXXX 2003, indicates that public prosecution was launched against several suspects including XXXX XXXX, on allegations that they distributed leaflets in order to facilitate the actions of illegal organizations. It states that according to article 168/2 of the Turkish Penal Code, these individuals were charged with being indirect members of the illegal organization of PKK. The decision concludes with stating that, "after considering the trial, the defense of the suspects and the whole contents of the file, that an amendment was made under the second subsection of law 4963 and article 169 of the Turkish Penal Code, phrase 'facilitating the actions of an illegal organization' was removed from the article which resulted in acquittal of the suspects: "Therefore in the circumstances, after the amendment was made to article 169 of the Turkish Penal Code, suspects with those activities did not commit the crime of Aiding and abetting and therefore all suspects ONE BY ONE WERE ACQUITTED."

As stated earlier, the birth date of the XXXX XXXX as indicated in the above decision is that of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX1981, born in XXXX however the birth date for the claimant's brother, XXXX XXXX as stated in his PIF is XXXX XXXX XXXX/1982 and his birth place in XXXX. The claimant subsequently provided an amendment to this information in XXXX 2013 indicating that his brother XXXX was born on XXXX XXXX XXXX/1981. The claimant was not questioned regarding the difference in birth dates and places of birth (XXXX as opposed to XXXX) and consequently, I have not drawn negative inference against the claimant's credibility on this point.

The relevance of this document; however, is that the decision clearly demonstrates that a 'XXXX XXXXwas provided a lawyer and that he along with others went to court and a trial was held due to his having been charged. On balance, in the absence of any charges being laid against this particular claimant before me, I do not find it credible that he was of any particular interest to police or that if he had indeed been suspected of supporting an illegal organization, as he has alleged. Rather I find it is more likely than not, that charges would have been laid against him similar to that of this XXXX XXXX, and others as stated in the country condition documentation indicate.17

Counsel again questioned the claimant regarding his not having any official document from the police to show that he had been detained. The claimant responded, "The Turkish police don't give you proof even though my father signed a paper. Also we were afraid to ask for it." Although counsel's subsequent questions indicated that the claimant never had criminal charges laid against him, nor was he interviewed by a public prosecutor, nor taken to court, the above decision, provides evidence to demonstrate there was due process in Turkey available for those suspected of collaborating with an illegal organization ensuring operational adequacies in place to protect the rights of those who had been arrested, charged and/or detained. If the above named XXXX XXXX is the claimant's brother, and if he was indeed the subject as named in the above decision, the claimant's evidence none-the-less indicates that this same brother remains in Turkey today, notwithstanding difficulties in having been suspect of terrorist activity in the past.

I accept that Turkish security forces, including police do detain Kurds, including BDP members, of which the claimant alleges to have supported, with links to the separatist Kurdish rebels.18 However notwithstanding mixed evidence regarding the treatment of Turkey's Kurdish population, the evidence clearly shows that the PKK is considered as a 'terrorist organization' by the government, and that a wider crackdown against the outlawed Kurdish rebels and their supporters began in 2009.19 Notwithstanding mixed country condition documentation20 including that provided by counsel, I find that there is legal and judicial address for those arrested, charged and detained on accusations of ties with outlawed Kurdish rebels including, most recently as at July 2012: "On July 2, 2012, a mass trial opened in Turkey of 205 suspects - many of whom remain at large - are on trial accused of links with the Union of Kurdistan Communities (KCK), which the authorities say is the urban wing of the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), part of a wider crackdown against what Ankara considers "terrorists" and their supporters. On July 13, 2012, an Istanbul court freed 16 suspects who are accused of ties with outlawed Kurdish rebels and had been in preventative custody for months, the state-run Antolia agency said. Among the 16 was Prof. Busra Ersani, a prominent political scientist at Marmara University, against whom the prosecution has requested a sentence of 15 years for belonging to a "terrorist organization."

Although the claimant alleges that this last detention precipitated his flight from Turkey, he did not experience any problems with security officials when he departed Turkey, eight days after he was allegedly detained and tortured in XXXX 2011. Given evidence provided in country condition documentation, particularly those pointed out by counsel in submissions,21 I do not find it credible that the claimant would have been able to pass through security checkpoints at the airport, using his own identity documents as testified if he was indeed of interest to any state authority. The claimant testified that the airport officials checked the computer files when he passed through them after reviewing his identity documents. I find on a balance that the claimant's ability to exit Turkey without difficulty particularly when questioned by security is inconsistent with allegations of being of any interest to Turkish authorities and thus impugns the credibility of his allegations.

Further, the claimant was questioned at length regarding which identity documents he provided to security at the airport when he departed in XXXX 2011. I found the claimant's responses evasive. Initially, when asked to detail his departure at the airport in XXXX 2011, the claimant did not respond to the question posed but replied, "On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, I was detained and beaten and tortured, including falaka." When asked if he had to present any documentation to security officials, at first he replied, No." When questioned as to whether he had to present a passport, the claimant replied, "I was asked for my passport, ticket and National Identity Card." When asked what identification he actually presented, the claimant replied that he provided his National Identity card, reiterating that he had no problems and was allowed to pass through security, after questioning.

Given country condition documentation regarding22 which states specifically that "departing flight passengers must have a valid passport to leave Turkey and a visa for the country to which he or she plans to travel which must be in the passport", I am on balance, unable to find it credible that the claimant did not present a passport when he departed in XXXX 2011. When questioned by counsel, the claimant maintained that he had no trouble at the airport because "the agent arranged everything." However, this is inconsistent with evidence which indicates that the individual must present "his or her own passport and ticket."

The claimant's evidence as indicated in his PIF at question 14 is that he departed Turkey using a passport in his own name however he does not list the serial number of the passport used or indicate when this passport was issued. When questioned regarding when this passport was issued, the claimant indicated that he had applied for and was issued this passport prior to the XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 incident however there was no evidence to indicate how it was that he had obtained it improperly. The claimant was asked about this new passport that he had allegedly obtained in 2011. Q Tell me about your final departure from Turkey. A On XXXX XXXX, 2011 I was detained. I got beaten and tortured including falaka. Q I asked about your departure from Turkey not the XXXX 2011 incident. A I left Turkey on XXXX XXXX, 2011; I was in Ismit and left from Istanbul which is one hour away. Q Did you have to provide any documents to security at the airport? A No. Q You did not have to present a passport? A I was asked for my passport, identification and airline ticket. Q What identification did you present? A Turkish National Identity card Q Did you experience any problems? A No, I showed them and was able to pass through.

Firstly, country condition evidence23 indicates that a person must apply in person and not through an agent at the passport office of the police headquarters in the city or are in which he/she lives and that checks are made to verify whether the person has any criminal convictions and/or is wanted by authorities. Clearly, the claimant would not have been issued a passport in 2011, if the police were indeed interested in him for any reason, including any prior detentions.

If the claimant did in fact use this passport which he states allegedly "improperly obtained",24 the fact remains that his name would still have been checked against a centralized computer system when he allegedly departed Turkey in XXXX 2011 to see if he was wanted for anything. In addition to finding on balance that the claimant's allegations that he is wanted by state authorities is inconsistent with his not being stopped or taken into custody by security at the airport, the claimant indicated that he returned this passport to the smuggler who assisted him.

The absence of this alleged new passport issued sometime in 2011 which the claimant alleges to have returned to the smuggler does not provide sufficient or reliable evidence to show that the claimant actually acquired a new passport. Passport issued in XXXX 2010

The only passport before the panel is a certified copy of the claimant's passport issued in his own name on XXXX XXXX, 2010 which he provided to CIC after he had made his intention known that he wished to claim refugee protection. I note that the issuance date was two days after he finished high school.25 Indeed, this is the only evidence before the panel which places the claimant in Turkey. I accept that the claimant was in Turkey in XXXX 2010; however, I have not been provided with reliable or credible evidence to demonstrate the claimant was in Turkey after that time.

Of concern is that there is only one stamp appearing in this passport: a visa stamped XXXX Ankara XXXX appearing on page 59. The claimant indicated that it was the presence of this stamp in his passport which made him apply for the new passport sometime after his failed attempt to leave Turkey in either the Fall of 2010, as indicated in his initial PIF or on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, as amended later. The claimant explained that he did not want to use a passport that had a stamp in it to indicate that his visa application had been refused. I am unable to find that this provides sufficient or satisfactory explanation of reasons the claimant would need to apply for a new passport.

The claimant was asked about his departures from Turkey and the process he followed at the airport. Q Tell me about your trip to Venezuela. A One agent, me and five others went to Venezuela through Italy to come to Canada. We were not allowed into Venezuela. We did not exit from the airport in Venezuela. Q How did you leave Turkey? A XXXX XXXX, 2011. Q What passport did you present? A The first one. Q The passport issued in XXXX 2010? A Yes. Q Was it stamped? A Yes. Q Who stamped it? A The police officer.

Given the claimant's testimony and issuance of this passport two days after completing high school, I find on balance that this would have been the passport that the claimant would have used to depart for Venezuela in the Fall of 201026 or in XXXX 2011, as per his amended PIF received in XXXX 2013. However, there are no departure nor re-entry stamps to corroborate the claimant's allegations regarding his attempt to flee to Venezuela in the Fall of 2010 or XXXX 2011 and his being denied entry to that country nor his re-entry to Turkey. Although country documentation indicates that exits from Turkey are not always indicated by way of passport stamps, the claimant when specifically questioned as to whether his passport was stamped when he exited for Venezuela testified that the police stamped his passport. The absence of any stamp in this XXXX 2010 issued passport by Turkish authorities undermines his credibility given that the only stamp present is the above-noted visa stamp.

Further, the claimant has provided a copy which is listed in the index of "Claimant's Personal Evidence III"27 at item two, as an "airplane ticket - Turkey to Venezuela, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011." However, I note that this is not an airline ticket but the purchase of an airline ticket which does not demonstrate that it was used by the claimant. Further, this ticket does not provide reasons for the claimant's having stated in his initial PIF that he had left for Venezuela in the Fall of 2010 or his having indicated to immigration officials that he visited Venezuela in either 2009 or 2010. It is noteworthy that the claimant indicated to immigration officials that his date of travel was one of two years - that is: 2009 or 2010. However neither 2009 nor 2010 reflects the year 2011, the year to which the claimant amended in his PIF nor the date of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 as stated on the purchased ticket. Consequently, the panel does not have any reliable evidence to show that the claimant departed Turkey in 2010 or 2011 for Venezuela other than his evidence that he did so. The claimant's explanation for the inconsistent dates was because his travel to Canada was difficult and long. I do not accept this explanation given that his PIF was completed with present counsel, over one month after he arrived to Canada. At best, I find that what the evidence does indicate is that the claimant had a desire to leave Turkey which provides reasons he applied for a passport a few days after he graduated from high school. This does not however in itself provide motivation for having acquired a passport or his attempt to leave Turkey at that time.

Having reviewed the claimant's circumstances in XXXX 2010, it is reasonable to infer that the reason for his wishing to leave was not due to his having been detained in either 2006 or 2009 given the almost two year delay in departure since his last detention. The relevance of discussing the claimant's failed attempt to depart Turkey is due to the claimant's inconsistent testimony regarding what indeed occurred at the airport when he departed at that time or his alleged subsequent return. Although he stated that this passport was stamped upon exit, as stated above, there is no exit stamp to show that it was stamped thus there is no credible or reliable evidence show when the claimant left Turkey. In addition, it is difficult to believe that which the claimant states because his credibility is impugned by inconsistencies. Alleged Passport and alleged return of passport to Agent upon arrival to Canada

The claimant indicated that he had applied for a new passport, because the Canadian Embassy stamped his first passport and therefore he was unable to use it to apply for any visas.28 The claimant stated in his narrative that his father knew an agent given his experience in helping the claimant's brothers leave Turkey.29 He was advised by the agent that he could take the claimant when he was taking others abroad. I find it interesting that the claimant indicated that his decision to leave Turkey was made at some point after (my emphasis) his failed attempt to enter Venezuela in the Fall of 2010 or XXXX 2011 but previous (my emphasis) to the March 2011 Newroz celebration, when he was allegedly picked up by police. Clearly, given the chronology as outlined in paragraph 12 of his narrative, the claimant had already applied for a new passport previous to the Newroz celebrations. There is no mention of using a smuggler or agent. However, the claimant has indicated in his PIF and reiterated in testimony that this passport had been "improperly obtained." When questioned regarding what documents he had to provide in order to get this new passport, the claimant replied that his father gave the agent for ID and photos, "that was all." I find that the claimant was attempting to maintain in testimony that the passport was obtained improperly by the agent who acquired it, even though this is inconsistent with country condition documentation which indicates that acquiring a passport needs to be done in person by the individual requesting it. None-the-less, the claimant maintained that he departed Turkey in XXXX 2011 using a passport issued under in his name.30 When asked where this new passport was today, the claimant testified that, "the agent took it. He made us give him all identity documents, including his Turkish Identification Card" (my emphasis). Notwithstanding the claimant's testimony that he gave his Turkish Identity card to the agent who assisted him to leave Turkey, the panel has a copy of the claimant's national Turkish Identity card provided by CIC. Although this inconsistency was not put to the claimant, it does demonstrate another instance of corroborative evidence before the panel which in the case of the absence of an exit stamp to show when he left Turkey the first time or in this latter instance, a copy of the claimant's National Identity card. As this was not put to the claimant I do not draw negative inference against his credibility on this point however, I am unable to find it credible, as stated earlier that the claimant would have been able to leave Turkey regardless of whatever identity document he presented, whether passport or National Identity card, if he was indeed wanted due to his political activities. Military Conscription

The claimant fears that he will be detained if he returns to Turkey because he "escaped the country and because he will be required to do military service which means he will be forced to commit violence. Given the claimant's age, his completion of high school in XXXX 2010 and having reviewed military conscription requirements in Turkey,31 the claimant was asked if as a young male, was it not mandatory that he serve in the military. He replied, "I didn't want to do it." When asked if he was required, he said, "I was but my school postponed it for me while I was a student." The claimant was asked if he had to provide documentation at the airport to show that he was exempt from military service. He testified, "I was given a paper and also I took university entry exams." The claimant was asked when it was that he was given a paper excluding him from military service. He replied that he was given it in 2010 however the panel does not have any corroborative evidence regarding this. When asked about this, the claimant testified that he asked his brother to get another copy of it for him so he could present it for his hearing. When asked if he had to provide any document to security officials at the airport upon departure to show that he was exempt from military service, the claimant replied, "It shows in the system so you don't have to prove anything." His further clarification indicated that airport officials checked the computers at the airport and that he waited for a few hours but there were no problems because the agent arranged everything.

The military exemption document provided by the claimant indicates it is from the Ministry of Defense, Military Draft Office, and is dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012, some 17 months after the claimant allegedly departed Turkey in XXXX 2011. It states that he was exempt from military procedure until the date XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX2014. The claimant was again asked reasons for the basis of his military exemption. The claimant repeated that he did not want to serve. When asked why it was that he did not go, the claimant replied, "I was still a student." It was pointed out to the claimant that his PIF indicates that he was not a student after XXXX 2010. The claimant replied, "When I came I was in school so I was probably wrong." There was however no evidence that the claimant attended school after having graduated in XXXX 2010. The claimant first indicated that he had written university entrance exams when questioned by counsel regarding his having attended a military draft office. The claimant was asked by the panel if he attended this office in XXXX 2011 when he turned 20 years of age. He indicated that he did and that he showed them a paper which indicated that he attended school, reiterating that he was still a student. I find that there has not been presented any credible or reliable evidence to show that the claimant was considered a student in XXXX 2011.

In the absence of any corroborative or reliable evidence to show that the claimant was a student in 2011, I assign more weight to that as stated in his PIF which indicates that he ceased attending school in XXXX 2010. Clearly, given the claimant acquired a passport in XXXX 2010 a few days after completing high school, and his evidence which indicated that he had left Turkey for Venezuela in the Fall of 2010, or XXXX 2011, I find that the claimant's actions are inconsistent with someone attending school. The claimant when questioned on this point simply testified that he did not want to attend university due to problems at universities in Turkey. When the panel pointed out to the claimant that he was not a student after he completed high school in XXXX 2010, the claimant maintained that he was still a student when he attended the military branch office in XXXX 2011. I find this adversely affects his credibility.

Further the claimant's employment history32 shows consistent employment in the XXXX industry from XXXX XXXX, 2010 until XXXX XXXX, 2011, nine days previous to his alleged departure on XXXX XXXX, 2011. I find on balance that the claimant had no intention of attending school in Turkey; that he did not attend further schooling after high school and that he was therefore not a student at the time he departed Turkey both the first time in the Fall of 2010 or XXXX 2011 nor when he departed in XXXX 2011. Given the absence of any indication in his PIF that he had written university exams which may have been reason for military deferral and the absence of any reliable evidence to show that he attended this military branch for the purposes of deferring this mandatory requirement, I am unable to assign any weight to the claimant's testimony stating he attended this office in XXXX 2011 which resulted in receiving exemption from military service. His allegations to the contrary consequently impugn his credibility.

In responses to questions regarding military exemption, according to the claimant's story, he was not questioned about a requirement for military service by airport or security officials when departing because according to the claimant, they checked the computers or because the agent was a rich man who had arranged everything. Whether the claimant was a student or not, in the absence of the alleged new passport, to indicate that the claimant was a student, as was indicated in his passport issued in XXXX 2010, as well an absence of information provided by CIC regarding any application for a Canadian student visa in his name to enter Canada, and the absence of any evidence to show that the claimant had problems entering Canada, I find on balance it reasonable to conclude that the claimant had acquired the requisite travel visa to enter Canada on this new passport which he indicated he had applied for previous to the Newroz celebration in March 2011 and his father's making arrangements with an agent. The absence of this passport does not provide evidence that he did not use it to travel into Canada legally. Corroborative evidence33 provided by the claimant with attached copy of DHL envelope, postmarked XXXX XXXX, 2012.

The claimant has provided a document, discussed above, regarding a deferral from military conscription,34 until XXXX XXXX, 2014, which he testified was procured by his brother who attended the military draft office to get it. I do not find it credible that the claimant's brother would be able to attend a military office to obtain confirmation that the claimant was exempt from military service unless he presented some documentation to show that he was exempt. According to the above document the claimant had received a roll call on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010 because it states he completed high school on XXXX XXXX, 2010 which resulted in his being given a deferral date until XXXX XXXX, 2013. The claimant however completed school on XXXX XXXX, 2010 and therefore was not a student as of that date. While he may have written university entrance exams which may provide reason for his been identified as a student on his XXXX 2010 passport, this notice from the military indicates that he is exempt only until XXXX XXXX, 2014. Letters provided by the claimant

In addition, the claimant has provided a letter with translation from the BDP detailing problems his family experienced, particularly a brother by the name of XXXX who was an XXXX member and another brother, XXXX who was detained during his university days. This undated letter allegedly from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in the town of XXXX indicated that the claimant was "detained 2 or 3 times due to his political activities", describing his being "subject to police beatings and pepper spray"35 which "caused various problems for many Kurdish youth as well as for XXXX." I assign little weight to this letter given it is undated and has been written in hand on paper without official BNP letterhead, notwithstanding it is allegedly from the Chairman of the BNP in the town of XXXX.

As well the claimant has provided a letter from his half-brother, XXXX, which although dated XXXX XXXX, 2012, does not provide helpful information particular to the claimant's circumstances, except to state that, "...On XXXX XXXX XXXXpolice raided our home as well and they ransacked our home. Police detained me. I remained in custody for two days and police asked me many questions about you. Police asked me if you have any connection with PKK abroad and what kind of activities you do there. You are very lucky you saved yourself. I hope you will be allowed to live there and you will not face the cruelty we face all the time..."36

I note that this particular sibling of the claimant, according to information provided in the claimant's PIF, would have been 19 years of age when this letter was composed. There is no indication as to reasons why this brother was detained, whether he was working, attending school, in the military or exempt from the military requirements. I assign little weight to this letter given that it sheds little light into reasons why this brother was asked questions about the claimant or why it would be that they would consider the claimant having possible connections with the PKK abroad. It would appear from this letter that the police knew that the claimant was abroad, which is reasonable given he was cleared through security at the airport at the time of his departure in 2011. However, I find it unreasonable that the Turkish authorities would all of a sudden have interest in the claimant's alleged connection to the PKK in XXXX 2012, one and one half years after the claimant was allegedly last detained in XXXX 2011. Further, I find it strange that this letter does not speak of the police asking about other brothers during this alleged XXXX 2012 detention, particularly those remaining in Turkey, in particular the claimant's brother who held XXXX office. I cannot attach weight to a document that was written one and one half years after the claimant's departure, given all the credibility concerns with the claimant's evidence in this area. I find that this letter is an attempt to bolster the claimant's claim and draw negative inference against the claimant's credibility.

Consequently, I do not find that the claimant has established a political profile or even a perceived one. I do not believe that the events occurred as relayed by the claimant, particularly the claimant's testimony regarding his having been detained and tortured ("falaka") during his last detention on XXXX XXXX, 2011, for reasons as discussed above.

More notable in my view, is that security officials at the Istanbul airport did not prevent the claimant's departure on XXXX XXXX, 2011. However the claimant's evidence on this point was inconsistent. Initially, the claimant when questioned by the panel testified that he experienced no difficulties with security officials when departing even though he testified that he was questioned by them and presented them with his Turkish Identification. In response to counsel's questions on this point, the claimant reiterated that he experienced no difficulties because "everything had been arranged by the agent." Counsel then asked the claimant if the agent was with him at the airport. The claimant replied that the agent was with him at the airport.

Given the inconsistencies regarding who presented which identity documents to security officials at the Istanbul airport and the evasive responses regarding whether the claimant was asked questions by security officials with respect to military exemption, I am unable on balance to assign any weight to this aspect of the claimant's testimony. Rather based upon the evidence before me, I am only able to find that the claimant experienced no difficulties with Turkish authorities at either of the times he departed Turkey which weighs negatively against his allegation that Turkish authorities had or continue to have any interest in him due to his political activities.

I find the claimant's attempts to testify otherwise and presentation of documentation in attempts to show continued interest by Turkish authorities in him negatively impugns his credibility such that I am unable to find no credible or trustworthy objective evidence to show that Turkish authorities had any interest in the claimant as at his departure at some point after his passport was issued in XXXX 2010 or in XXXX 2011 or XXXX 2011. Further, I have considerable concerns regarding the claimant's delay in claiming protection at the first available opportunity which is inconsistent with some one fearing persecution. My reasons follow. Alleged Travel Route to Canada

The claimant departed from Istanbul, Turkey on XXXX XXXX, 2011 by plane. According to his first PIF, he arrived in Cuba on XXXX XXXX, 2011 by way of Madrid, Spain. He remained in Havana, Cuba for 1 1/2 months after which he travelled to Nassau, Bahamas where he remained from XXXX XXXX, 2011 until he left for West Palm Beach, Florida on XXXX XXXX, 2011, where he remained for 3 days before traveling to Detroit. He crossed the border into Windsor, Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2011 in the trunk of a truck and made his claim for protection at an inland immigration office on XXXX XXXX, 2011. The amended PIF indicates that he stayed in Cuba for 2 weeks and 2 months in Nassau before going by boat to Florida.

If the claimant did depart Turkey in XXXX 2011, which I do not have sufficient evidence to persuade me is the case, I find it unreasonable that the claimant did not seek protection at the earliest opportunity after he departed Turkey. Although I can give the claimant benefit of doubt with regards to not seeking protection in Spain given it appears to have been a transit country to Cuba, I am unable to accept that the claimant did not seek protection in Cuba, Nassau or the United States. I can appreciate that he has brothers in Canada, but he does also have a brother in the United States.

The claimant's not availing himself of protection in the United States impugns his credibility. However, I note that the panel has not been presented with sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence to show that the claimant arrived in the United States when he stated he did. The above negative inferences against the claimant's credibility of allegations and absence of corroborative evidence to show when he arrived in the US or Canada for that matter, does not provide the panel with any comfort in believing anything the claimant has stated. The claimant could have arrived in Canada 2010 along with a cousin who made a successful claim for protection or he could have remained in the United States for longer than he has stated in his original PIF.37 The problem is that the panel has not been provided sufficient credible or reliable evidence to show where the claimant actually was after XXXX 2010.

While I can appreciate that the claimant would feel more comfortable in coming to Canada because he has two brothers and a cousin in this country, that in of itself does not mean the claimant should not have or could not have taken the opportunity to advance a claim in the United States and await his determination given his life was at risk based on the problems as described.

On the issue of not claiming in the United States, the panel notes the following Federal Court of Canada case law, Matos Quintana,38 which states: Considering the obvious lack of credibility regarding the event at the centre of the claim, it was not unreasonable to not grant any probative value to all the documents submitted by the applicant. (XXXX XXXX XXXX) (3) It was not unreasonable to determine that the fact that the applicant did not claim refugee status in the United States-a country where he spent three months and for which he had a five-year visa-could undermine his credibility. Similarly situated persons

The claimant has two brothers who have been accepted as Convention refugees in Canada and another who made a successful asylum claim in the U.S.39 While there is an IRB notice of decision for the brother who arrived in 2005 to show that he was determined a Convention refugee on December 20, 2007, there is no similar notice of decision regarding the brother who arrived in 2002. However, counsel has provided a sworn declaration from him indicating that he was determined to be a Convention refugee in February 2003.40 In addition, the claimant has a third brother who made an asylum claim in the U.S. as indicated in his PIF who was accepted on a asylum application on May 24, 2004.41 A cousin, XXXX, arrived to Canada in 2010 and was accepted as a Convention refugee in April 2011.42 I note that the claimant indicated that he was in Cuba in XXXX 2011 and that he subsequently left there by plane to the Bahamas where he remained until XXXX XXXX, 2006 before taking a boat to West Palm Beach, Florida. I believe that had the claimant really suffered the persecution alleged, he would have been interested in any safe destination outside Turkey, at the earliest time. I find that the subjective fear of the claimant comes into question with his actions and testimony. By definition, a Convention refugee is someone who has a well-founded fear of persecution. Fear is, by its very nature, subjective, while the well-foundedness of that fear is an objective matter. Both subjective and objective components are required to meet the definition.43 A lack of evidence going to the subjective element of the claim is in itself sufficient for the claim to fail.44 Given the claimant had brothers who had made successful refugee claims both in Canada and the U.S., I am unable to find his delay in making his intention known to claim protection earlier than at an inland office on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 is inconsistent with a subjective fear. Finding

A claimant's contradictory testimony can cast doubt upon the totality of his oral evidence.45 As a result, I do not find that the claimant has established a political profile, or even a perceived one. I do not believe that the events occurred as relayed by the claimant, as I do not find that the claimant has provided credible or trustworthy evidence that he was in Turkey at the time of the precipitating incident. Indeed there has been no credible or reliable evidence to show that he was in Turkey after XXXX 2010. At minimum, the claimant could have asked his brother, XXXX XXXX, who allegedly employed the claimant from XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010 to XXXX XXXX, 2011. Given the claimant has provided letters from either brothers, I find it unreasonable not to have some record or corroborative evidence to support he worked for this company which would have place him in Turkey after XXXX 2010. More so, given XXXX is the brother who sent documents the claimant provided in Personal Evidence II.46
I do not find the claimant is a person of interest with the Turkish police. I do however believe that he is Kurdish and that he is subject to military conscription as other Turkish citizens.

I accept that certain high profile, politically active Kurds, and especially leaders of the Kurdistan Worker's Party (PKK) could have severe problems with the Turkish government. However, this claimant has not established this profile.

There is no evidence that the Kurds are persecuted as an entire group, and while their situation has been problematic, especially in regions in the south eastern Turkey where they are the majority, and fighting continues with the Turkish military47 and while there may be discrimination of Kurds in Turkey; the treatment of the Kurdish population has improved. The Kurdish population is estimated to 10-23% of Turkey's entire population. It is the largest linguistic and ethnic minority and millions of Kurds from the south eastern region have resettled in larger western cities, like Istanbul, Ankara and Mersin and integrated well.48
One important cultural celebration is Newroz, and it is noted in the evidence that in 2008 approximately 180 events occurred across the country and they were generally peaceful.49

Improvements in Turkey with respect to recognizing the cultural aspirations of Kurds have included, in 2006, a change to allow Kurdish language publications and television broadcasts and in 2008, a law allowing state-owned television to broadcast in Turkish.50

Finally, it is noted that the claimant had no trouble getting a passport issued and left the country without any issues. Objectively, we know that passport applicants are subject to thorough investigations and entries and exits are checked for criminality.51 There are no indicators that the claimant is of interest to the police for any reason. Military Evasion and Conscientious Objection

With respect to the claimant's military objection, the claimant states that he is a conscientious objector and that he fears the military in Turkey for what would be his refusal to serve on grounds of conscience as he does not want to kill anyone, including Kurds and that he would be persecuted as a result. However, I note there is no reference to being a conscientious objector in the "Claim For Refugee Protection In Canada" document, particularly question 43 which asks, "Why are you asking for Canada's protection?"

I note that the claimant completed and signed the declaration which was also signed by the Turkish interpreter on XXXX XXXX, 2011 indicating that the claimant understood the nature and effect of the information provided which includes a) the verbal exchange between the officer and the claimant during the examination; b) the content of the forms identified by the officer and c) the content of the declaration. While I accept that the immigration interview is meant to provide brief details of reasons for fearing to return to Turkey, I do not find it reasonable for the claimant not to have included this in his fear of returning to Turkey when presented with the opportunity.

The claimant fears that he will be mistreated for his military evasion. Incidents in Turkey of harassment and discrimination of the Kurds do exist according to the documents, and while inexcusable and unpleasant, this does not meet the threshold of persecution. The definition is forward-looking, and the risk must be assessed in accordance with events in Turkey today.

This claimant alleged he was deferred military service due to having written university acceptance exams which resulted in a deferral until 2014. However, the claimant indicates that he left in XXXX 2011 even though there were no indicators that he was attending university. As a citizen of Turkey the claimant is able to have his military service deferred until age 39.

In a Response to Request for Information,52 there is no alternative to military service in Turkey. The following is stated: Those draftees who are not ready for military service have to submit their documents showing the reasons (being a student, being unable to perform military service due to health reasons, being in prison, etc.). If these persons fail to report to their military branches, they become yoklama kaçagi (pre-registration draft evaders) as of November 1st of that year. Draftees who complete their final military draft registrations join the military during the year that they become 21 years old. Those who do not attend to the call of the military branches or those who fail to join the related military training center or unit after completing their registrations become bakaya (post-registration draft evaders). Once the government is aware of those who have become yoklama kaçagi or bakaya, their name and address is forwarded to the security authorities (the police or gendarme) by the administrative authorities (the governorships) and consequently, security authorities are authorized to begin to search for these persons. Simultaneously, the military branches of the persons in question send an official letter to their address, stating that they have become draft evaders and that they have to apply to their military branch to complete the relevant procedures. (Turkey 6 May 2010) According to the Official, draft evaders (both yoklama kaçagi and bakaya) are not allowed to travel abroad until they legalize their situation (ibid.). WRI similarly indicates that draft evaders cannot leave Turkey, and that customs, immigration and police officers would be aware that they are evading military service (WRI 23 Oct. 2008). Forum 18, a Norwegian and Danish non-profit organization promoting the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion (Forum 18 n.d.), reports that in an attempt to prevent the cycle of prosecutions against conscientious objectors, the Turkish Ministry of Justice issued a decree on 3 July 2008 which states that deserters can only be arrested with a court warrant by the police and not by the military recruitment office (17 Mar. 2010). Further information on the decree could not be found among the sources consulted by the Research Directorate within the time constraints of this Response.

I accept that Turkey does not have an alternative to military service for those who genuinely object in serving or a process to legitimately examine the genuineness of such a military objection by virtue of conscience. However, this is a decision made by the government officials of Turkey which is an operation of law. I have not been provided with sufficiency of evidence that would indicate that the prosecution of the claimant for failing to comply with a military order, if such an order exists, would amount to persecution.

In Hinzman,53 the Federal Court stated the following: My conclusion in this regard is reinforced by the recent decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Ates v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2005] F.C.J. No. 1661. In Ates, the Court stated that even in a country where military service is compulsory and where there is no alternative to military service available, the repeated prosecutions and imprisonments of a sincere conscientious objector does not amount to persecution on a Convention ground. If persecution does not arise in the circumstances described in Ates, then surely the prosecution and potential imprisonment of a volunteer soldier by a country that does provide some, albeit limited, alternatives to military service would similarly not amount to persecution on a Convention ground.

Given the concerns raised in this claim as it addresses the credibility of the evidence, the panel was not sufficiently convinced that the claimant encountered problems as alleged and that he suffered and would continue to suffer persecution as a result if required to return to Turkey.
The claimant has the responsibility to prove he has an objectively identifiable risk in Turkey and keeping in mind the Convention definition. The claimant has not met his burden, in the panel's view.

Simply, after reviewing all the evidence, inclusive of counsel's submissions as it pertains to a well-founded fear of persecution or that the claimant is in need of protection pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA, there has not been a successful argument made to suggest a positive determination in this regard.

In Li,54 the Federal Court stated, "pursuant to subsection 97(1), there must be persuasive evidence, that is on a balance of probabilities, establishing the facts on which a claimant relies, to say that he or she faces a substantial danger of being tortured on his or her return. Second, the danger or risk must be such that it is more likely than not that he or she would be tortured or subjected to other cruel or other degrading treatments." This is not the case in this claim.

In Bouaouni,55 the Federal Court stated "a claim under section 97 must be evaluated with respect to all the relevant considerations and with a view to the country's human rights record." In evaluating this claim under section 97 and considering the human rights record of Turkey, I have not been persuaded that the claimant would face a substantial danger of being tortured, or that the risk and/or danger is such that it would be more likely than not that the claimant would be tortured or subjected to cruel or other degrading treatments, based on what has already been mentioned earlier in these reasons.

Having considered all the evidence, inclusive of the documentary evidence and the submissions from the claimant's counsel, I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as he has not established that there is a reasonable chance or serious possibility that he would be persecuted for a Convention ground or there would be a risk to his life or he would be subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should he be required to return to Turkey in a forward looking analysis. On substantial grounds, there is no danger of torture should the claimant return to Turkey.

Therefore, I reject this claim pursuant to both sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.
